issues.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right of redemption is not extinguished merely because a mortgagee exercises a power of sale and sells the mortgaged property at auction; it continues until the sale is completed by a registered conveyance.
material_facts: The society mortgaged its land and incomplete building under a mortgage deed conferring a power of sale without court intervention.
After the society failed to pay the mortgage debt, the mortgagee advertised and held a public auction, and the appellant was declared the highest bidder.
The appellant paid the purchase price and took possession, but no registered conveyance completing the sale had been executed.
The society paid the mortgage debt to the mortgagee before completion of the sale and sought to redeem the property.
issues.conclusion: The auction and the contract of sale did not extinguish the society’s right of redemption; because the sale had not been completed by a registered conveyance, the society could redeem on payment of the amount due.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 54 and 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a contract for sale does not itself transfer an interest in the property, and the right of redemption continues unless extinguished by an act of the parties or a court decree. Read with section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, transfer of the mortgagor’s interest in immovable property requires a registered instrument; the right is therefore not extinguished by the mortgagee’s auction or by a mere contract for sale. Section 69(3) protects a purchaser’s title from challenge on the ground that no case authorising the sale had arisen, but does not make an auction contract a completed transfer. The Court approved Abraham Ezra Issac Mansoor v. Abdul Latif Usman and Ellappa Naiker v. Sivasubramania Maniagaran, and rejected the contrary view in Meenakshi Velu v. Kasturi Sakunthala. The English decisions in Waring v. London and Manchester Assurance Co. and Property & Bloodstock Ltd. v. Emerton were distinguished because they rested on section 100(1)(i) of the English Law of Property Act, 1925.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a mortgagor may redeem mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_public_auction: The mortgagee exercised a power of sale by putting the mortgaged property up for public auction.
predicates.no_registered_conveyance: No registered conveyance completing the transfer of the mortgagor’s interest had been executed.

issues.definition: When a mortgage redemption dispute involves a mortgagee’s public auction and no registered conveyance has been executed, the mortgagor retains the right to redeem.

issues.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not create a property interest in the proposed purchaser under Indian law.
material_facts: The mortgagee sold the property at auction under a power contained in the mortgage deed.
The appellant was declared the highest bidder and paid the purchase price, but the conveyance had not been completed by a registered instrument.
The appellant argued that the auction contract transferred an interest in the property, relying in part on English decisions.
issues.conclusion: The auction contract did not give the appellant an interest or right in the property that extinguished the society’s equity of redemption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, expressly provides that a contract for sale does not of itself create any interest in or charge on the property. Indian law does not recognise the English distinction between legal and equitable estates in land; there can be only one owner, the legal owner. The Court followed Rani Chhatra Kumari v. Mohan Bikram and Rambaran Prasad v. Ram Mohit Hazra, and distinguished the English decisions because they applied a different statutory framework.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_dispute: The proceeding concerns the sale of immovable property and the rights asserted by a proposed purchaser.
predicates.sale_contract_only: The proposed purchaser’s claim to the property rests on a contract of sale.
predicates.no_completed_transfer: The transfer of ownership has not been completed by the legally required instrument.

issues.definition: When an immovable-property sale dispute rests only on a sale contract and the transfer has not been completed, the proposed purchaser acquires no property interest from that contract.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee exercising its own power of sale acts under a right adverse to the mortgagor, not as the mortgagor’s agent.
material_facts: The mortgage deed authorised the mortgagee to sell the property without court intervention in specified circumstances.
The mortgagee exercised that power after the society failed to pay the mortgage debt.
The appellant argued that the mortgagee’s power was an agency coupled with an interest and that the auction sale should be treated as an act of the mortgagor.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagee’s sale was an exercise of its own right against the mortgagor and could not be treated as an act by the mortgagor that extinguished the right of redemption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the mortgagee’s right to sell under the mortgage deed is distinct from, and adverse to, the mortgagor’s rights. The mortgagee is not acting as the mortgagor’s agent when exercising that power. Accordingly, the mortgagee’s auction or the resulting sale contract does not itself constitute an act of the mortgagor extinguishing redemption under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

predicates.mortgage_power_sale_dispute: The proceeding concerns the effect of a mortgagee’s exercise of a power to sell mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_exercised_own_sale_power: The mortgagee conducted the sale by exercising a power granted to it under the mortgage.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a mortgagee’s power of sale and the mortgagee exercised its own sale power, the sale is not treated as an act of the mortgagor.
